title: Impacts of Artificial Lighting on Human Behaviour In-Office Buildings—A Systematic Literature Review
authors: Mohamed Salaheldin Amin Mohamed et al., 2024
review_question: To examine the effects of artificial lighting on office workers, providing a comprehensive overview of existing research, including different types of artificial lighting and their impacts on workplace behaviour such as productivity, mood, and health.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Included: Empirical studies published in English (Jan 2018-Apr 2023) from Scopus, focusing on lighting effects on human behaviour in administrative office settings. Dependent variables must measure physical, psychological, or social well-being. Independent variables must relate to artificial lighting. Excluded: Non-administrative office settings (mining, healthcare, factories), theoretical/technological/non-empirical papers, studies lacking transparent data collection/analysis, studies focused on job satisfaction/motivation, or those related to natural light.

findings.consequent: Worker performance, productivity, energy efficiency, colour control, durability, visual comfort, alertness, mood, well-being
findings.quote: LED lighting demonstrates superiority over fluorescent lighting in enhancing worker performance and productivity due to its innovative features and potential benefits on circadian rhythm regulation, emotional responses, cognitive performance, and visual comfort.

findings.antecedent: Artificial lighting characteristics (spectral composition, CCT, illuminance, dynamic patterns)
findings.consequent: Circadian rhythms, melatonin regulation, sleep quality, mood, emotional responses, cognitive performance, concentration, productivity
findings.quote: The impact of artificial lighting types on human behaviour encompasses a wide array of physiological and psychological dimensions... Circadian rhythms... are profoundly influenced by the spectral composition of artificial lighting.

findings.antecedent: Inadequate or inappropriate artificial lighting (e.g., excessively high/low illuminance, poor quality)
findings.consequent: Eye strain, visual discomfort, hampered task engagement, diminished productivity, negative effects on sleepiness, vitality, mood, reduced work engagement
findings.quote: Conversely, inadequate lighting can lead to eye strain and visual discomfort, hampering task engagement.
cooler lighting promoting alertness and warmer lighting evoking relaxation.

findings.consequent: Alertness, mood, cognitive performance, visual comfort, glare indexes, sleep quality
findings.quote: Dynamic lighting during the daytime can improve alertness and mood, potentially reducing feelings of sleepiness, while at nighttime, it can lead to a decrease in perceived sleep quality and sleep time.

findings.antecedent: Glare factors (absolute luminance, illuminance values, relative contrast)
findings.consequent: Physiological and ocular responses (Pupil Diameter, Pupillary Unrest Index, Blink Rate, Blink Amplitude), visual discomfort
findings.quote: glare factors, both absolute (luminance and illuminance values) and relative (contrast), can predict physiological and ocular responses, such as Pupil Diameter (PD), Pupillary Unrest Index (PUI), Blink Rate (BR), and Blink Amplitude (BA).

findings.consequent: User acceptance, perceived colour quality, colour rendition
findings.quote: the colour rendering index (CRI) and correlated colour temperature (CCT) of lighting can indeed affect user acceptance in-office settings.

synthesis_conclusions: LED lighting demonstrates superiority over fluorescent lighting in enhancing worker performance and productivity due to its innovative features and potential benefits on circadian rhythm regulation, emotional responses, cognitive performance, and visual comfort.
Artificial lighting has a range of effects on human behaviour, encompassing circadian rhythm regulation, emotional responses, cognitive performance, and visual comfort.

Optimizing correlated colour temperature (CCT) to align with cooler colours, reducing glare through proper lighting design, and ensuring high colour rendering index (CRI) values can collectively enhance worker productivity and well-being in the workplace.

Maintaining illuminance levels at an appropriate balance, considering both the intensity and quality of light, contributes to creating an environment that fosters optimal performance and positive employee experiences.
Productivity studies highlight the nuanced effects of illuminance on alertness, mood, and sleep, while dynamic lighting control demonstrates the potential for cognitive performance enhancement.
Mood and emotional well-being analyses underline the importance of user preferences in dynamic lighting's impact.
Lighting's role in circadian rhythms and preventing health issues emerges as vital.
evidence_gaps: Small sample sizes and limited participant diversity in many studies.
Issues with evaluation methods and data analysis (e.g., privacy concerns with Digital ID).
Lack of consideration for temporal variables (e.g., morning vs. afternoon effects on working memory).
Insufficient distinction between sunlight and artificial light during illuminance measurements.
Limited deep investigation into the impact of lighting glare and Colour Rendering Index (CRI) on human behaviour, visual performance, and comfort.
Ethical considerations and experimental design issues need addressing.
limitations: The review focused on peer-reviewed articles from a single database (Scopus), potentially limiting the scope of included academic work.

Future research could benefit from broadening the scope to include other types of academic work (e.g., doctoral dissertations, research reports) and using more specialized databases (e.g., Web of Science Core Collection, PsycINFO, PubMed).
Gaps in sample sizes, participant diversity, evaluation methods, and data analysis persist in the existing literature.
